name: Source Authority & Credibility Hierarchy

tiers.label: Authoritative Primary Truth
categories: Official language and runtime specifications (ECMAScript, ISO C++, W3C, RFCs)
Primary documentation portals (docs.rs, docs.python.org, nextjs.org/docs, react.dev, developer.mozilla.org)
Official framework API schema registries and OpenAPI specifications

tiers.label: Canonical Evolution & Maintainer Releases
categories: Official GitHub releases, CHANGELOG.md, and upgrade guides authored by maintainers
Direct commits to main/master in maintainer-owned repositories
Official RFC PRs and core maintainer architectural proposals

tiers.label: Maintainer Issue Trackers & Empirical Bug Reports
categories: Closed GitHub issues with merged fix commits or verified maintainer workarounds
Open GitHub issues with reproducible minimal reproduction repositories
Core team member technical write-ups and release announcements

tiers.label: Independent Engineering Deep-Dives
categories: Engineering blogs of established tech companies (Cloudflare, Netflix, Uber, Vercel engineering)
Reproducible independent benchmarks with published hardware, versions, and test scripts
Vetted community packages and established maintainers

tiers.label: Unverified Community Content (Distrust by Default)
categories: StackOverflow questions and answers (frequently obsolete or version-mismatched)
Medium, Dev.to, and personal developer blogs (often copy-pasted without testing)
Reddit discussions, Hacker News threads, and Discord forum summaries

discreditedSources.description: Never adopt technical solutions, API signatures, or architecture recommendations from these sources without Tier 1 verification
sources: AI-generated search overview snippets (Google SGE / Bing Copilot summary excerpts)
SEO content aggregator farms (GeeksForGeeks, Baeldung, Tutorialspoint, Javatpoint)
Outdated documentation for previous major versions without a version banner
Marketing landing pages claiming performance or zero-cost without reproducible benchmarks

operationalRules: Always prefer a Tier 1 or Tier 2 source over any combination of Tier 5 sources
A single snippet from Tier 5 is insufficient evidence to adopt a code pattern
When Tier 1 documentation and a community blog contradict, Tier 1 always prevails
If an API appears in a Tier 5 source but cannot be located in Tier 1 or 2, treat it as a probable hallucination or deprecated legacy API
